questions.stem: The INDIAN STOCK MARKETS are regulated by:

options.option_text: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
Finance Ministry directly
SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India; set up 1988, given statutory powers by SEBI Act 1992; HQ Mumbai; also regulates mutual funds, FPIs, REITs, InvITs
NITI Aayog

questions.explanation: SEBI (SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE BOARD OF INDIA) — regulator of securities and capital markets in India. ESTABLISHED: (a) Non-statutory body on 12 APRIL 1988 by Government of India resolution; (b) Became STATUTORY (autonomous) under SEBI ACT 1992 after the HARSHAD MEHTA ‘1992 scam’ (fraudulent use of bank receipts on BSE — ₹5,000 crore); (c) HQ at MUMBAI (BKC); 4 regional offices (Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Ahmedabad). OBJECTIVES (‘mandate’): (1) PROTECT INTERESTS of investors in securities; (2) PROMOTE development of securities markets; (3) REGULATE securities market. POWERS: (a) quasi-legislative (frame rules/regulations — SEBI Takeover Code, LODR, ICDR etc.); (b) quasi-executive (investigate, issue orders); (c) quasi-judicial (adjudicate through SEBI whole-time members). COMPOSITION: Chairman + 2 whole-time + 2 part-time members (appointed by GoI). CURRENT CHAIRPERSON (as of Apr 2026): TUHIN KANTA PANDEY (ex-Finance Secretary, took office March 2025, replacing Madhabi Puri Buch who was India’s first female SEBI chair). ENTITIES SEBI REGULATES: (1) STOCK EXCHANGES — BSE, NSE, MSEI, commodity exchanges (MCX, NCDEX); (2) ISSUERS of securities (IPOs, FPOs, rights issues); (3) INTERMEDIARIES — merchant bankers, brokers, sub-brokers, registrars, depositories (NSDL, CDSL); (4) FOREIGN PORTFOLIO INVESTORS (FPIs); (5) MUTUAL FUNDS; (6) ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT FUNDS (AIFs) — PE, VC, hedge funds; (7) REITs & InvITs (Real Estate + Infrastructure Investment Trusts); (8) CREDIT RATING AGENCIES (CRAs — CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings); (9) INVESTMENT ADVISERS; (10) RESEARCH ANALYSTS; (11) PORTFOLIO MANAGERS. NOT REGULATED by SEBI: banks (RBI), insurance (IRDAI), pensions (PFRDA), government bond issuance (RBI on behalf of GoI). FSDC — Financial Stability and Development Council — apex inter-regulatory body (Finance Minister chairs) to coordinate among RBI-SEBI-IRDAI-PFRDA.

questions.stem: The BENCHMARK stock index representing 30 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) is:

options.option_text: NIFTY 50
SENSEX
NASDAQ Composite
Dow Jones

questions.explanation: SENSEX (‘SENSitive indEX’) — India's OLDEST benchmark stock market index; tracks 30 LARGE, WELL-ESTABLISHED, actively-traded, financially sound companies representing diverse sectors on the BOMBAY STOCK EXCHANGE (BSE). Full name: S&P BSE SENSEX. HISTORY: (1) BSE established 1875 — ASIA's OLDEST stock exchange; (2) SENSEX launched 1 Jan 1986; (3) Base year 1978-79, Base value 100; (4) methodology shifted to FREE-FLOAT market capitalisation weighting in Sept 2003. SIGNIFICANT MILESTONES: (a) First crossed 1,000 in 25 July 1990; 5,000 in Oct 1999; 10,000 in Feb 2006; 20,000 in Oct 2007 (pre-GFC peak); 25,000 in 2014; 50,000 in Jan 2021; 60,000 in Sep 2021; 75,000 in Apr 2024; 80,000+ by 2025. (b) Sensex touched ~85,000 in late 2024 before correction. COMPUTED EVERY 15 seconds during trading hours (9:15-15:30 IST). NIFTY 50 — India's other benchmark, on the NSE (NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE, founded 1992, operational 1994, now world's biggest derivatives exchange by volume). Nifty 50 is a 50-stock index launched 1996; base year 1995, base value 1000. Currently in the ~25,000 range (2026). OTHER INDIAN INDICES: (1) BSE SMALLCAP, MIDCAP, LARGECAP; (2) BSE 100, BSE 200, BSE 500; (3) NIFTY NEXT 50, NIFTY MIDCAP 50/100/150, NIFTY SMALLCAP; (4) SECTORAL — BANK NIFTY, NIFTY IT, NIFTY PHARMA, NIFTY AUTO, NIFTY FMCG, NIFTY METAL, NIFTY REALTY; (5) BSE DOLLEX (US-dollar version). GLOBAL INDICES: DOW JONES INDUSTRIAL AVERAGE (30 stocks, USA, oldest — 1896); S&P 500 (USA, 500 stocks); NASDAQ Composite (tech-heavy, USA); FTSE 100 (UK, London); DAX 40 (Germany); NIKKEI 225 (Japan); HANG SENG (Hong Kong); SHANGHAI COMPOSITE; KOSPI (Korea); STRAITS TIMES (Singapore); ASX 200 (Australia). free-float market-cap weighted; base year 1978-79, base value 100; launched 1986; also called BSE 30, or S&P BSE SENSEX.

options.option_text: A bond issue by the government
The FIRST SALE of shares to the PUBLIC by a private company
The buyback of shares by a company
A central bank open-market operation

questions.explanation: IPO (INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING) — the FIRST TIME that a private company offers its SHARES to the PUBLIC to raise capital. After the IPO, the company becomes ‘PUBLIC / LISTED’ and its shares are traded freely on stock exchanges. CLASSIFICATION of markets: (1) PRIMARY MARKET — where securities are ISSUED for the first time (IPO, FPO, rights issue); company receives the money. (2) SECONDARY MARKET — where PREVIOUSLY-ISSUED securities are traded among investors (regular stock exchange trading); company doesn't receive proceeds, but buyers/sellers transact. IPO PROCESS (India, SEBI ICDR Regulations 2018): (a) appoint MERCHANT BANKERS (book-running lead managers — BRLMs); (b) DRHP (Draft Red Herring Prospectus) filed with SEBI; (c) SEBI approves after scrutiny; (d) RHP (Red Herring Prospectus) finalised; (e) SUBSCRIPTION period: 3-5 working days; (f) PRICE BAND set (e.g., ₹100-105); investors bid in BOOK-BUILDING process; (g) ALLOTMENT on pro-rata basis; (h) LISTING DAY — shares begin trading. Categories of investors in an Indian IPO: QIB (Qualified Institutional Buyers, 50% in book-built) - institutional investors like MFs, FIIs, banks, insurance; NIIs (Non-institutional investors, 15%) — individuals with application > ₹2 lakh; RETAIL (35%, typically) — individuals up to ₹2 lakh; EMPLOYEE reserve portion. Types of offering: FRESH ISSUE (new shares, cash goes to company) or OFFER FOR SALE (OFS, existing shareholders sell — cash goes to them, not to company). ANCHOR INVESTORS — get allotment 1 day before public subscription. IPO TERMS: (1) LISTING — inclusion on stock exchange; (2) LOCK-IN — existing shareholders may be restricted from selling for 6-18 months; (3) GREY MARKET PREMIUM (GMP) — informal pre-listing trading price; (4) LISTING GAIN — difference between IPO price and listing-day price. FAMOUS IPOs in India: (a) COAL INDIA 2010 (₹15,475 cr, was largest till 2021); (b) LIC 2022 (₹21,008 cr, India's largest IPO ever); (c) PAYTM 2021 (₹18,300 cr, notorious for post-listing losses); (d) ZOMATO 2021 (unicorn IPO era); (e) HDFC BANK, TCS (multi-decade wealth creators). FPO = Follow-on Public Offering (already-listed company raises more capital). OFS (Offer for Sale, separate mechanism for promoters to sell shares to public via SE). the company ‘lists’ on a stock exchange; raises primary-market capital; regulated by SEBI (ICDR Regulations).

options.option_text: Falling prices, pessimistic outlook
RISING prices, OPTIMISTIC outlook (vs BEARISH = falling, pessimistic); bull attacks by thrusting horns UPWARD, bear swipes paws DOWNWARD
High interest rates
Illegal insider trading

questions.explanation: BULL vs BEAR — classical stock market terms. BULL / BULLISH: (a) Market is RISING / prices are going UP; (b) investors OPTIMISTIC about future; (c) buying interest dominates. Etymology: a bull attacks by thrusting its HORNS UPWARD — stock prices move UP like a bull's strike. A ‘BULL MARKET’ = prolonged rise of 20%+ from lows; some last years. BEAR / BEARISH: (a) Market is FALLING / prices going DOWN; (b) investors PESSIMISTIC; (c) selling pressure dominates. Etymology: a bear attacks by swiping paws DOWNWARD. A ‘BEAR MARKET’ = prolonged decline of 20%+ from highs. OTHER MARKET ANIMAL ANALOGIES: (1) CHICKEN — panicky investor selling out of fear; (2) PIG — greedy investor taking excessive risk; ‘bulls make money, bears make money, pigs get slaughtered’; (3) SHEEP — herd-following investor; (4) OSTRICH — investor ignoring bad news (‘head in sand’); (5) DOVE / HAWK — policy stance of central banks (dove = accommodative, hawk = tight); (6) WOLF — aggressive predatory trader (‘Wolf of Wall Street’ book/film about Jordan Belfort); (7) WHALE — very large investor. OTHER STOCK MARKET TERMS: (a) BLUE CHIP — very well-established, high-market-cap, stable company (e.g., TCS, RIL, HDFC Bank, ITC, HUL); (b) PENNY STOCK — very low price (<₹10), small-cap, risky; (c) GROWTH STOCK — high earnings growth, reinvests; (d) VALUE STOCK — undervalued relative to fundamentals; (e) DIVIDEND STOCK — pays high/regular dividends; (f) MULTIBAGGER — returns multiples of investment (10-bagger = 10x return); (g) BOURSE — alternative term for stock exchange; (h) CIRCUIT BREAKER / CIRCUIT FILTER — automated trading halt when market moves beyond set % (SEBI: 10%, 15%, 20% levels in Sensex/Nifty); (i) UPPER CIRCUIT / LOWER CIRCUIT — when a single stock moves by a preset %; (j) SHORT SELLING — selling borrowed shares with expectation of buying back cheaper; (k) F&O — Futures & Options (derivatives). (l) VIX — Volatility Index (‘Fear Gauge’); Nifty VIX reflects expected volatility over next 30 days.

questions.stem: The DEPOSITORIES that hold Indian investors' shares in DEMATERIALISED (demat) form are:

options.option_text: Only NSE's depository
NSDL (National Securities Depository Ltd, promoted by IDBI/UTI/NSE, 1996) and CDSL
Only SBI banks
Physical vaults of RBI

questions.explanation: DEPOSITORIES in India — institutions that hold securities (shares, bonds, ETFs, mutual fund units) in ELECTRONIC / DEMATERIALISED (‘DEMAT’) form, replacing physical paper share certificates. TWO depositories exist: (1) NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) — established 1996 (India's FIRST depository); promoted by IDBI Bank, UTI, NSE; HQ Mumbai; (2) CDSL (Central Depository Services Limited) — established 1999; promoted by BSE and leading banks; HQ Mumbai. Both regulated by SEBI under the DEPOSITORIES ACT 1996. DEMAT ACCOUNT holds securities; investors access it via a DEPOSITORY PARTICIPANT (DP) — usually a broker (Zerodha, Groww, Angel One, ICICI Direct, HDFC Securities, Kotak) or bank. BENEFITS of DEMAT: (a) no forgery / theft / loss of certificates; (b) no stamp duty on transfer (except 0.015% for delivery); (c) fast settlement — T+1 (since Jan 2023) and T+0 in pilot (2024 onwards); (d) easy corporate actions (dividend auto-credit, bonus/split/rights auto-applied); (e) secure pledging/loan against shares. Securities TRACED end-to-end: issuer company → RTA (Registrar + Transfer Agent — KFintech, Link Intime) → Depository (NSDL/CDSL) → DP → investor's demat account. SETTLEMENT CYCLE — T+1 (trade date + 1 working day), moved from T+2 in 2023; T+0 same-day settlement in pilot phase for select stocks. GLOBALLY: T+1 is standard in USA (since May 2024), EU moving to T+1 by 2027. Depositories outside India: DTCC (USA), Euroclear + Clearstream (Europe), JASDEC (Japan), KSD (Korea). MARKET INFRASTRUCTURE INSTITUTIONS (MIIs) under SEBI: stock exchanges (BSE, NSE, MSEI, commodity exchanges), depositories (NSDL, CDSL), clearing corporations (ICCL, NSCCL) — they are ‘systemically important’. RECENT INDIAN MILESTONE: NSDL's IPO expected 2025-26; CDSL already listed in 2017 (the first Asian depository listed). DEMAT ACCOUNTS in India: crossed 20 CRORE in early 2025 (vs 4 crore in 2020), growth driven by fintechs + WFH trading. both regulated by SEBI; Central Depository Services Ltd, promoted by BSE, 1999.

questions.stem: A MUTUAL FUND pools money from many investors to invest in:

options.option_text: Only government bonds
Only equity shares
A DIVERSIFIED PORTFOLIO of stocks, bonds, and other securities
Real estate exclusively

questions.explanation: MUTUAL FUND (MF) — investment vehicle that pools money from many investors to invest collectively in securities (stocks, bonds, money market, gold, derivatives). Managed by a professional FUND MANAGER on behalf of the investors; each investor owns UNITS (proportional shares) of the fund's portfolio. Indian MFs regulated by SEBI under the MUTUAL FUND REGULATIONS 1996. AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India) is the industry body. STRUCTURE: (1) SPONSOR — company that establishes the MF (e.g., HDFC, ICICI Prudential, SBI). (2) TRUSTEES — hold fund assets in trust for unitholders. (3) AMC (Asset Management Company) — manages the fund, takes investment decisions; licensed by SEBI. (4) CUSTODIAN — holds the actual securities. (5) RTA — maintains investor records. TYPES OF MFs: (A) BY STRUCTURE: (1) OPEN-ENDED — units can be bought/sold anytime at NAV; no fixed maturity (most common). (2) CLOSE-ENDED — fixed tenure, units issued at launch only, listed on exchange. (3) INTERVAL — hybrid. (B) BY ASSET CLASS: (1) EQUITY — primarily stocks (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, multi-cap, ELSS, sectoral, index); (2) DEBT — primarily bonds (liquid, gilt, corporate bond, credit risk, dynamic bond); (3) HYBRID — mix (balanced, aggressive hybrid, conservative hybrid, multi-asset); (4) SOLUTION-ORIENTED — retirement, children; (5) OTHER — GOLD ETFs, international, FoF (fund of funds). (C) BY MANAGEMENT STYLE: (1) ACTIVELY MANAGED — fund manager picks stocks, higher expense ratio; (2) PASSIVELY MANAGED / INDEX FUND — tracks an index like NIFTY 50 or SENSEX; lower expense ratio; (3) ETFs — Exchange-Traded Funds traded like stocks. KEY TERMS: (a) NAV (Net Asset Value) — per-unit value of the fund = (total assets − liabilities) / units outstanding; (b) ENTRY LOAD (abolished by SEBI 2009); (c) EXIT LOAD — charged if redeemed within a period; (d) EXPENSE RATIO — annual fees as % of AUM (capped by SEBI); (e) AUM (Assets Under Management) — total value managed; (f) SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) — periodic (monthly) investment of fixed amount, averages cost via RUPEE-COST AVERAGING. INDIAN MF industry AUM: ~₹62 lakh crore (late 2024), monthly SIP inflows ~₹25,000 cr. ELSS = Equity Linked Savings Scheme — 3-year lock-in, 80C deduction. FAMOUS AMCs: SBI MF, HDFC MF, ICICI Prudential, Nippon India, Kotak, Axis, UTI, Aditya Birla SL.

questions.stem: ‘DERIVATIVES’ in financial markets include instruments like futures and options, whose VALUE is DERIVED FROM:

options.option_text: The price of the paper on which they are printed
The performance of the regulator
An UNDERLYING ASSET
The market capitalisation of all listed stocks

questions.explanation: DERIVATIVES — financial CONTRACTS whose VALUE is DERIVED FROM an UNDERLYING ASSET (stock, index, commodity, currency, bond, interest rate, or another derivative). They allow investors to: (1) HEDGE — reduce risk of adverse price moves in the underlying; (2) SPECULATE — bet on future price movements with leverage; (3) ARBITRAGE — exploit price differences across markets. FOUR MAIN TYPES: (I) FORWARDS — OVER-THE-COUNTER (OTC), CUSTOMISED contract between two parties to buy/sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date; unregulated; counterparty risk. (II) FUTURES — standardised, EXCHANGE-TRADED version of forwards; mark-to-market daily; margin-based; eliminates counterparty risk via CLEARING HOUSE. Types: STOCK FUTURES (on individual shares), INDEX FUTURES (Nifty 50, Sensex), CURRENCY FUTURES, COMMODITY FUTURES, INTEREST RATE FUTURES. (III) OPTIONS — contract giving BUYER the RIGHT (not obligation) to buy/sell an asset at a STRIKE price on/before an EXPIRY date; SELLER has the OBLIGATION. CALL OPTION = right to BUY; PUT OPTION = right to SELL. Buyer pays a PREMIUM to seller. TYPES: European (exercise only on expiry), American (any time up to expiry). IN-THE-MONEY (ITM), AT-THE-MONEY (ATM), OUT-OF-THE-MONEY (OTM). The OPTIONS GREEKS: Delta (sensitivity to underlying), Gamma, Vega (volatility), Theta (time decay), Rho (interest rate). (IV) SWAPS — contracts to EXCHANGE future cash flows; INTEREST RATE SWAP (fixed for floating), CURRENCY SWAP, CREDIT DEFAULT SWAP (CDS — famously at centre of 2008 GFC). INDIAN DERIVATIVES MARKET: (a) Equity F&O introduced June 2000; NSE now the world's LARGEST derivatives exchange by volume (2022, overtook CME). (b) Currency F&O — USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR, JPY/INR. (c) Commodity exchanges: MCX (metals + energy — gold, silver, crude, natural gas), NCDEX (agri — wheat, soybean, cotton); regulated by SEBI since 2015 (earlier by FMC). (d) SEBI reforms 2024 — weekly expiries reduced to 1 per exchange per week to curb retail speculation. (e) 2024 DATA: retail F&O traders LOST ₹1.8 lakh crore cumulatively over 3 years (SEBI study). (f) STT (Securities Transaction Tax) on F&O. LEVERAGE — derivatives allow control of large positions with small margin; hence high gain potential but equally high loss potential. Famous derivative disasters: Barings Bank (Nick Leeson, 1995), LTCM (1998), Lehman Brothers (2008), Archegos (2021). value fluctuates based on underlying's price; used for hedging, speculation, arbitrage; stock, index, commodity, currency, bond, interest rate.

questions.stem: The ABBREVIATION ‘P/E’ (as in ‘this stock has a P/E of 25’) stands for:

options.option_text: Price-to-Employees ratio
PRICE-to-EARNINGS ratio
Profit-to-Equity ratio
Performance-to-Expectation index

questions.explanation: PRICE-TO-EARNINGS RATIO (P/E or PE ratio) — one of the most widely used STOCK VALUATION metrics. Formula: P/E = CURRENT SHARE PRICE / EPS (Earnings Per Share). EPS = Net Profit / No. of outstanding shares. Interpretation: (a) P/E = 25 means investors are paying ₹25 for every ₹1 of annual earnings the company generates; (b) equivalently, at current earnings, it would take 25 years for the company to ‘earn back’ the purchase price; (c) HIGH P/E (say 40-50+) — expensive vs earnings; may indicate GROWTH expectations (market expects future earnings to explode); or OVER-VALUATION; (d) LOW P/E (say 8-10) — cheap; UNDER-VALUATION, OR slow-growth/risky company; (e) NEGATIVE P/E — company has losses. USE: (i) COMPARE a stock to its PEERS within the same sector (Banking stocks typically trade at lower P/E than IT/Pharma); (ii) compare with HISTORICAL AVERAGE P/E of the same stock; (iii) compare with the INDEX P/E (Nifty 50's long-run average P/E ~20-22; if above 28 seen as expensive). TYPES: (A) TRAILING P/E — uses past 12 months actual EPS; (B) FORWARD P/E — uses estimated next-year EPS; (C) SHILLER P/E (CAPE) — cyclically adjusted, uses 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings — popular for long-term macro valuation. OTHER key FINANCIAL RATIOS for investors: (1) P/B (Price-to-Book) — share price / book value per share; for banks this is often more used than P/E; <1 = potentially undervalued; (2) DIVIDEND YIELD = DPS / share price (%); (3) ROE (Return on Equity) = Net Profit / Shareholders' Equity; measures profitability on investor capital; >15% = good; (4) ROCE (Return on Capital Employed); (5) EV/EBITDA — Enterprise Value / Earnings Before Interest-Tax-Depreciation-Amortisation; for capital-intensive companies; (6) DEBT-TO-EQUITY — borrowings / equity; high = risky; (7) CURRENT RATIO — short-term assets/liabilities, liquidity; (8) QUICK RATIO — excludes inventory; (9) INTEREST COVERAGE — EBIT/Interest expense. PEG RATIO (P/E divided by annual earnings growth %): <1 = fair; 1-2 = okay; >2 = expensive. Peter Lynch popularised it. MARKET CAP = share price × total shares; categories: LARGE (top 100 in India ~>₹20,000 cr), MID (101-250), SMALL (beyond). market price per share ÷ earnings per share (EPS); indicates how many years of earnings investors are willing to pay for the stock; high P/E = growth expectation or over-valuation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the OLDEST stock exchange in Asia?

options.option_text: BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange) — founded 1875 as ‘The Native Share & Stock Brokers' Association’ under a banyan tree on Dalal Street, Mumbai; Asia's OLDEST
Tokyo Stock Exchange
Hong Kong Stock Exchange

questions.explanation: BSE (BOMBAY STOCK EXCHANGE) — ASIA'S OLDEST stock exchange; located at DALAL STREET, MUMBAI. HISTORY: (1) Founded in 1875 by PREMCHAND ROYCHAND and 21 others as ‘THE NATIVE SHARE AND STOCK BROKERS' ASSOCIATION’; initial gatherings were under a BANYAN TREE opposite Mumbai's Town Hall (later at Dalal Street). (2) Recognised under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 — became India's FIRST exchange to be granted permanent recognition by the GoI. (3) Corporatised and demutualised in 2005 (Demutualisation Scheme). (4) Listed on itself in 2017. CURRENT FACTS: ~5,300 listed companies (most of any exchange globally), market cap > $5 trillion. CEO: Sundararaman Ramamurthy. Trading platform: BOLT (BSE on-Line Trading, now BOLT Plus and new-gen). SENSEX is BSE's flagship index. BSE has also launched: INDIA INX (India International Exchange) at GIFT City, Gujarat (2017) — India’s first international financial services exchange. NSE (NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE) — India's larger and technologically more advanced exchange. FOUNDED: 1992 (under HARSHAD MEHTA scam aftermath — replacing open outcry with electronic trading); commenced operations 1994. INITIATIVES: (a) first to introduce SCREEN-BASED, ORDER-DRIVEN, anonymous trading (NEAT — National Exchange for Automated Trading) — revolutionised Indian markets; (b) first to launch DERIVATIVES in India (2000); (c) introduced NIFTY 50 in 1996; (d) NSE-promoted: NSDL (depository), NSCCL (clearing), NSE IFSC (GIFT IFSC, 2017). NSE holds ~93% market share of equity cash volumes in India, and is the WORLD'S LARGEST derivatives exchange by contracts traded (2022 onwards, overtook CME Group). NSE IPO: planned but delayed due to SEBI disputes (co-location scandal resolved 2023); expected 2026. OTHER EXCHANGES GLOBALLY: NYSE (New York, 1792 — founded under ‘Buttonwood Tree’ agreement, oldest in world), LSE (London, 1698), Tokyo (1878), Shanghai (1866, re-opened 1990), Hong Kong (1891), Nasdaq (1971, world’s first electronic exchange), Euronext (Paris-Amsterdam-Brussels merger). By MARKET CAP: NYSE (~$27T) > Nasdaq ($24T) > Shanghai, Tokyo, Euronext, HKEX, NSE India (~$4-5T, rising). In 2024, India briefly overtook HK to become 4th-largest market by cap.

questions.stem: BONDS (G-Secs, corporate bonds) are DEBT securities that REPRESENT:

options.option_text: Ownership stake in a company
A LOAN given BY the investor TO the issuer
A derivative contract
Units of a mutual fund

questions.explanation: BONDS — DEBT SECURITIES that represent a LOAN from an investor to a borrower (government, company, or municipality). The issuer agrees to: (a) pay PERIODIC INTEREST (‘coupon’) — usually semi-annually or annually; (b) return the PRINCIPAL (‘face value’/‘par value’) at MATURITY. Bonds are ‘FIXED-INCOME securities’. Unlike stocks (EQUITY — ownership stake), bondholders are LENDERS, NOT owners; they get priority over equity in case of liquidation. KEY BOND TERMS: (1) FACE VALUE (par) — principal to be repaid (often ₹1,000 or ₹10,000 in India); (2) COUPON — stated interest rate; (3) MATURITY — date of principal repayment; (4) YIELD TO MATURITY (YTM) — total return if held to maturity (incorporates coupon + price gap vs face); (5) CREDIT RATING — AAA (highest), AA, A, BBB (investment grade) ... D (default). Rated by CRAs: CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings (S&P, Moody's, Fitch globally). TYPES of bonds: (I) BY ISSUER: (a) SOVEREIGN / G-SECS — issued by Govt of India (via RBI); considered risk-free; T-bills (up to 1 year), Dated G-Secs (up to 40 years); regulated by RBI; traded on NDS-OM platform; cut-offs auctioned weekly. (b) STATE DEVELOPMENT LOANS (SDLs) — state govt bonds. (c) PSU BONDS — e.g., REC, PFC, HUDCO. (d) CORPORATE BONDS — private/listed firms. (e) MUNICIPAL BONDS — city governments. (II) BY FEATURE: ZERO-COUPON (no interim coupon, sold at discount); CALLABLE (issuer can redeem early); PUTTABLE (holder can redeem); CONVERTIBLE (can convert to equity — FCCB Foreign Currency Convertible, Optionally Convertible Debentures); PERPETUAL / AT-1 bonds (no maturity, Basel III bank tier-1 capital); GREEN bonds (funds environmental projects); SOCIAL bonds; SDG-linked; MASALA BONDS (rupee-denominated offshore bonds). INVERSE PRICE-YIELD: BOND prices move OPPOSITE to interest rates. When RBI raises rates, bond prices FALL (old bonds' fixed coupon less attractive); when rates fall, prices RISE. DURATION measures price sensitivity to rate changes. INDIAN BOND MARKET: (a) G-Secs market is well-developed, ~₹170 lakh crore outstanding; (b) Corporate bond market small (~₹45 lakh crore) but growing post-Ratan Tata Committee + SEBI reforms; (c) RBI RETAIL DIRECT (2021) — allows retail investors to buy G-Secs directly; (d) Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs, started 2015) — gold-denominated; 2.5% coupon; 8-year tenure; tax-free LTCG at maturity; paused in 2024-25 amid high gold prices; (e) JP Morgan + Bloomberg index INCLUSION of Indian G-Secs (June 2024) brings $25-40 billion inflows over 18 months. Taxation: interest on bonds taxed at slab rate; sovereign gold bonds tax-free at maturity. issuer pays periodic COUPON (interest) + returns PRINCIPAL at maturity; lower risk than equity; regulated by SEBI (corporate bonds) + RBI (G-Secs); government or company.

questions.stem: In an Indian IPO, 'ASBA' is the mandated payment mechanism where an investor's bid amount is blocked in their bank account until allotment. What does the acronym ASBA expand to?

options.option_text: Application Submitted through Bank Approval
Application Supported by Blocked Amount
Authorised System for Bid Allocation
Allotment Scheme for Blocked Applications

questions.explanation: B is correct: ASBA = Application Supported by Blocked Amount, introduced by SEBI in 2008. The bid money is blocked (not debited) in the investor's savings account, so they continue earning interest. Allotment happens first; only then is the amount debited. Option A ('Bank Approval') is a common confusion — 'blocked amount' is the defining feature, not a bank's approval of the bid.

questions.stem: An individual who wishes to distribute mutual fund products in India must obtain an ARN (AMFI Registration Number) after clearing the NISM-Series-V-A exam. AMFI stands for:

options.option_text: Association of Monetary and Financial Institutions
Association of Mutual Funds in India
Authority for Market Finance and Investment
Agency for Mutual Fund Intermediaries in India

questions.explanation: B is correct: AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India) was incorporated in 1995 as a self-regulatory organisation for the mutual fund industry; it issues ARNs to distributors. Option A ('Monetary and Financial Institutions') is a common mix-up that places AMFI in the banking sector rather than the asset-management space. AMFI is not a statutory regulator — SEBI holds that role.

questions.stem: Under SEBI's market-wide circuit breaker mechanism, if the Nifty 50 or BSE Sensex falls by 10% before 1:00 PM on a trading day, trading on all stock exchanges is halted for:

options.option_text: 15 minutes, after which trading resumes without any restriction
45 minutes, after which a pre-open call auction precedes resumption
The entire trading day, with no further resumption permitted
30 minutes, followed by a mandatory 15-minute cooling-off window

questions.explanation: B is correct: SEBI's circuit breaker circular specifies a 45-minute halt for a 10% index fall occurring before 1:00 PM; trading resumes after a pre-open session. Option A (15 minutes) is the rule for the same 10% trigger but only when the fall occurs between 1:00 PM and 2:30 PM — candidates often confuse the two time-band rules. A fall after 2:30 PM triggers no halt at all.

questions.stem: India migrated to a T+1 equity settlement cycle from January 2023. Under T+1, if a retail investor purchases shares on a Wednesday (a normal trading day), the shares are credited to their demat account on:

options.option_text: Wednesday itself, before the market closing bell of that session
Thursday, the very next trading day (T+1 business day)
Friday, two full business days after the purchase date
The following Monday, after the weekend clearing window closes

questions.explanation: B is correct: Under T+1, the clearing and settlement of both shares and funds happens on the next working day (Thursday). Option C (Friday) describes the earlier T+2 cycle that India phased out. India was the second major market after China to implement T+1, with SEBI mandating it in a phased rollout starting with the smallest 100 stocks in February 2022 and completing it for all listed securities by January 2023.

questions.stem: A company issues 'bonus shares' to its existing shareholders from accumulated free reserves. What is the key distinction between bonus shares and a 'rights issue'?

options.option_text: Bonus shares are allotted free by capitalising reserves; rights issue requires shareholder payment
Bonus shares are offered only to promoters; rights issue is open to all public shareholders
Bonus shares reduce the company's reserves to zero; rights issue creates fresh equity capital
Bonus shares require only SEBI approval; rights issue needs RBI clearance in addition

questions.explanation: A is correct: bonus shares capitalise free reserves (e.g., retained earnings) — no cash changes hands, the shareholder gets extra shares for free. A rights issue is a fresh fundraise where existing shareholders are given the right to subscribe to new shares at a discounted price; they must pay. Option B is wrong because bonus shares go to ALL registered shareholders in proportion to their holdings, not just promoters. Option D is wrong — both instruments fall under SEBI's purview, not the RBI.

questions.stem: Under the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations 2011, once an acquirer's holding crosses 25% of the voting rights in a listed target company, they must launch a mandatory open offer. The open offer must be made for a minimum of:

options.option_text: 20% of the total voting capital of the target company
26% of the total voting capital of the target company
51% minus the acquirer's existing shareholding percentage
15% of the non-promoter floating public shareholding

questions.explanation: B is correct: Regulation 7 of SEBI SAST Regulations 2011 mandates an open offer for at least 26% of total voting capital once the 25% trigger is breached. Option A (20%) is a persistent wrong answer — 20% was the open-offer size under the superseded 1997 Takeover Code, not the 2011 regulations. Option C (51% minus stake) conflates the takeover threshold with a majority-control formula — SEBI specifies 26% as an absolute minimum, not a residual calculation.

questions.stem: The 'Green Shoe Option' (GSO) in an IPO allows the stabilising agent to over-allot shares and subsequently buy them back from the secondary market to support the post-listing price. Under SEBI guidelines, the maximum permissible over-allotment through a GSO cannot exceed:

options.option_text: 10% of the total shares offered in the IPO issue
15% of the total shares offered in the IPO issue
20% of the total shares offered in the IPO issue
25% of the total shares offered in the IPO issue

questions.explanation: B is correct: SEBI's DIP (Disclosure and Investor Protection) Guidelines cap the Green Shoe Option at 15% of the total IPO issue size. The stabilising agent (typically the lead book-runner) can over-allot up to this limit; if the price drops below the issue price post-listing, it buys back shares to prop up the price, returning them to the issuer. Option A (10%) is the most common distractor — candidates confuse it with the anchor-investor lock-in relaxation or the minimum application lot percentage rules. The GSO is named after the US shoe company Green Shoe Manufacturing, the first firm to use this mechanism.
